rules.quote: Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity.
rules.specification: Check meaning-changing ambiguity, not merely whether a hyphenated alternative exists. Correct expressions with different meanings must not be treated as violations of one another. Use the more specific rules below when their structural conditions apply.
rules.violation_condition: An unhyphenated expression has an unintended plausible reading that a hyphen would distinguish from the intended meaning.
when: The intended meaning is recoverable from context.
A hyphen distinguishes the intended expression from another plausible reading.
This includes prefixes whose hyphenated and unhyphenated forms have different meanings.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates meaning-distinguishing prefix cases; E-1 keeps the contrasting correct forms compliant.

covers.quote: words of fewer than 6 letters
one-syllable words
2-syllable words.

rules.quote: Don’t break short words over a line
rules.specification: Use the three listed categories as the operational protected cases. The manual does not give an additional threshold for other words described as short.
rules.violation_condition: A short word is split across lines, including a word with fewer than 6 letters or with one or 2 syllables.
when: The text is being laid out for print.
A word is split at a line boundary.
The protected cases are alternatives: fewer than 6 letters, one syllable, or 2 syllables.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the listed categories as conditions of one line-breaking check.

rules.quote: Break words between syllables
rules.specification: Assess syllable and morpheme boundaries together. Prefer compound-component and base–affix boundaries; otherwise place the break before a consonant unless that split is misleading. The fragment before the break should help the reader anticipate the word.
rules.violation_condition: A word is divided across lines at an unsuitable boundary: inside a syllable, across an available compound or affix boundary, or at a point that makes the initial fragment misleading.
when: A word is being divided across lines in print.
The word is not protected by the short-word rule.
A break before a consonant is not preferred when it creates a misleading fragment.
rules.why: G-2 treats boundary selection and the misleading-fragment exception as one line-breaking check.

rules.quote: Don’t include extra hyphens if you need to break up URLs or email addresses.
rules.violation_condition: A URL or email address contains a hyphen inserted only to mark a line break, rather than a hyphen belonging to the address.
when: A URL or email address is broken across lines.
Hyphens that are genuinely part of the address are not prohibited.
rules.why: G-2 combines URLs and email addresses because the same inserted-character error is checked.

covers.quote: Sometimes a prefix such as ‘non-’, ‘pre-’ or ‘anti-’ acts on more than one word.

rules.quote: If the phrase is already hyphenated, use a second hyphen to link the prefix to all words in the phrase.
rules.violation_condition: A prefix acting on an entire already-hyphenated phrase is not joined to that phrase with a hyphen.
when: The prefix acts on more than one word.
The phrase to which the prefix applies is already hyphenated.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the scope and existing-hyphen conditions with the one missing-link check.

rules.quote: Use a hyphen when the last letter of a single-syllable prefix is a vowel and the word that follows begins with the same vowel.
rules.specification: The manual leaves the well-known-word exception open. A dictionary-backed exception list is needed; coordinate and cooperate are explicit unhyphenated exceptions.
rules.violation_condition: A single-syllable prefix ending in a vowel is joined without a hyphen to a base beginning with the same vowel, except for established unhyphenated words.
when: The prefix has one syllable.
The prefix's final vowel and the base's initial vowel are identical.
Well-known words can retain established unhyphenated spellings.
rules.why: G-3 records established spellings as exceptions; G-4 selects the actionable body sentence rather than the topic heading.

when: The capital letter starts the base word, not merely the whole expression at the start of a sentence.

rules.quote: Don’t use hyphens if the 2 words end and start with different vowels.
rules.specification: Read this in its prefix context. Different-vowel combinations are normally joined, but a single-syllable vowel-initial base takes a hyphen. The direction records the main prohibition; the explicitly stated exception also requires detection of a missing hyphen.
rules.violation_condition: A prefix and base meeting at different vowels have an unnecessary hyphen, or lack the exception's separating hyphen when the base has a single syllable.
when: A vowel-final prefix meets a base beginning with a different vowel.
A single-syllable vowel-initial base takes a separating hyphen.
Two-syllable prefixes are covered by their more specific rule.
Capital-initial, numerical and italic bases follow their specific prefix rules.

covers.quote: Two-syllable prefixes ending in ‘o’ are often attached without a hyphen, regardless of what the base word starts with.
Two-syllable prefixes ending in a consonant are rarely followed by a hyphen.

rules.quote: Two-syllable prefixes ending in a vowel other than ‘o’ and followed by another vowel are often hyphenated. If the base word begins with a consonant, the term is usually written as one word.
rules.specification: These are tendencies, not categorical spelling rules. Normally hyphenate a two-syllable prefix ending in a non-o vowel before a vowel; normally join it before a consonant. Prefixes ending in o or a consonant are normally joined. A dictionary-backed exception list is needed before treating individual forms as errors.

when: The prefix has 2 syllables.
Non-o vowel endings followed by a vowel generally take a hyphen.
Non-o vowel endings followed by a consonant generally form one word.
Prefixes ending in o generally form one word regardless of the base's first letter.
Prefixes ending in a consonant generally form one word.
More specific rules for capital letters, numbers, italics and meaning-distinguishing hyphens take precedence.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the ending-dependent cases; the interpretation preserves the manual's non-absolute wording.

when: Ex means former.
The requirement applies whether the base starts with a vowel or a consonant.
rules.why: G-2 retains the meaning and initial-letter conditions; the universal wording makes this a requirement.

when: The base following the prefix is a number or an italic expression.
The italic-expression case requires access to formatting.

rules.quote: Write most suffixes without hyphens
rules.specification: The listed common suffixes normally attach directly. The word 'most' leaves lexical exceptions unspecified; a dictionary-backed exception list is needed beyond the explicit -fold and -odd rules.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinary suffix is separated from its base by an unnecessary hyphen.
when: The ending functions as a suffix.
The common listed suffixes include -able, -ate, -ation, -fold, -ful, -ise, -ish, -ly, -ment, -ness and -y.
Numeral-plus-fold forms follow the specific -fold rule.
Forms ending in -odd follow the specific -odd rule.
Established lexical exceptions are excluded.
rules.why: G-4 merges the heading and body restatement; the specifically named suffix conventions retain their own checks.

rules.quote: A hyphen precedes ‘-fold’ when that suffix is used with a numeral, but not a spelled out number.
rules.violation_condition: The suffix fold lacks a hyphen after a numeral or has a hyphen after a spelled-out number.
when: Fold is a numerical suffix.
Numeral bases take a hyphen.
Spelled-out number bases do not take a hyphen.
rules.why: G-2 keeps numeral and spelled-out bases as conditions of one -fold check.

rules.quote: Always use a hyphen with the suffix ‘-odd’, whether it’s with a word or numeral.
rules.violation_condition: The suffix odd is attached to a word or numeral without a hyphen.
when: Odd functions as the suffix, not as a separate adjective.
Both word and numeral bases require the hyphen.
rules.why: G-2 combines both base forms; 'Always' establishes the stronger requirement.

examples.note: Both constructions are correct.

rules.quote: Hyphens link elements of compound words as a phrase, but usually only when they are used before a noun as adjectives. Don’t use hyphens when the phrase is after the noun in the sentence structure.
rules.specification: Apply the positional distinction to phrasal modifiers such as up to date and dusk to dawn. More specific rules for intrinsic compound adjectives, participles, set phrases, adverbial modifiers and marked expressions take precedence, preventing duplicate findings.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinary phrasal compound adjective is unhyphenated before its noun, or remains hyphenated as a phrase after the noun, outside the more specific compound conventions.
when: The expression is a multiword phrase functioning as a compound adjective.
Before a noun, the phrase is normally hyphenated.
After the noun, the phrase is normally unhyphenated.
Adjective-plus-adjective and noun-plus-adjective compounds retain their hyphens in either position.
Expressions governed by another specific compound rule are checked under that rule instead.
rules.why: G-2 combines the before/after conditions; G-4 absorbs the adverbial-phrase restatement without duplicating its positional check.

covers.quote: For adverb–verb combinations, you don’t need a hyphen.

Reverse-order exception.
Reverse-order exception.

The verb precedes the adverb.

covers.quote: Don’t hyphenate adverbial phrases when they play an adverbial role.

The only exceptions are 2 formations using the adverb ‘fully’:

rules.quote: Don’t use a hyphen in most compounds consisting of an adverb ending in ‘-ly’ and a participle (a part of a verb ending in ‘-ing’ or ‘-ed’).
rules.specification: Consolidate the page's repeated adverbial prohibition. Identify an actual adverbial relationship rather than relying on an -ly ending alone. Do not extend the final heading to prohibit every compound containing an -ing or -ed form.
rules.violation_condition: A hyphen joins an adverbial modifier to the word it modifies, especially an -ly adverb followed by a participle, except for fully-fashioned and fully-fledged.
when: The modifying word or phrase is functioning adverbially.
In particular, an -ly adverb modifies a participle.
Fully-fashioned and fully-fledged are explicit exceptions.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates repeated prohibitions; G-3 retains the named exceptions; the precise body wording limits the broad final heading.

covers.quote: Sometimes, you might need to use a hyphen for clarification.

rules.quote: Never use a hyphen for a compound modified by words such as ‘very’, ‘particularly’, ‘least’ or ‘most’.
rules.specification: The named words illustrate degree modification rather than an exhaustive lookup list. Preserve the subsequent clarification exception: more-experienced can distinguish greater experience from a greater number of experienced people.
rules.violation_condition: A compound modified by a degree word such as very, particularly, least or most contains an unnecessary hyphen.
when: A degree modifier modifies the compound.
A hyphen needed to distinguish the intended meaning is permitted by the subsequent clarification passage.
rules.why: G-3 retains the clarification exception; E-1 keeps both different-meaning staff examples compliant.

covers.quote: Set phrases
If the phrase is further modified, use a hyphen to prevent ambiguity.
